100867.heading: Generic Type Constraint
100867.content:
A generic type constraint limits which type arguments may replace a type parameter. A `where` clause can require a particular base class or interface, or distinguish reference types with `class` from value types with `struct`.

Constraints let generic code safely use members promised by the constraint instead of treating the parameter as an unconstrained unknown. Multiple compatible constraints can express a more precise contract for a [[Generic Type]] or [[Generic Method]].

100870.heading: Generic Method
100870.content:
A generic method declares one or more type parameters on the method itself, so it can reuse one algorithm across different statically checked types. The containing class does not need to be generic.

Constraints can state which operations the method requires, such as `IComparable<T>` for comparison. When arguments make the type unambiguous, C# type inference can supply the type argument at the call site.

100873.title: Generic Variance
100873.heading: Generic Variance
100873.content:
Generic variance describes when constructed generic interfaces or delegates remain assignment-compatible across an inheritance relationship. Covariance marks an output type parameter with `out`, while contravariance marks an input type parameter with `in`.

The direction reflects how the parameter is used: a covariant producer can supply a more derived result, and a contravariant consumer able to accept a base type can also accept values supplied through a more specific contract.

100876.heading: Target-Typed New Expression
100876.content:
A target-typed `new` expression omits the constructed type when the surrounding assignment or argument already determines it. For example, `Dictionary<string, int> scores = new();` avoids repeating the declared type.

The feature reduces syntactic duplication without weakening static typing: the compiler still resolves a concrete constructor from the target type. It is clearest when the target is visible and unambiguous near the expression.

100879.title: Compile-Time Error and Runtime Exception
100879.heading: Compile-Time Error and Runtime Exception
100879.content:
A compile-time error prevents source code from being successfully built, while a runtime exception interrupts a program after it has compiled and begun executing. The distinction identifies whether the compiler rejected the program or execution encountered a condition the running code could not continue through normally.

Exception handling addresses anticipated runtime failure paths. It cannot repair syntax or type errors that stop compilation before the program exists as an executable artifact.

100882.title: Exception Handling
100882.heading: Exception Handling
100882.content:
Exception handling gives a program explicit control paths for abnormal runtime conditions. In C#, `try`, `catch`, `throw`, and `finally` separate risky work, matching recovery logic, deliberate failure signaling, and cleanup that must occur regardless of outcome.

Handling is useful only when the program can add context, recover, clean up, or transfer responsibility to a more appropriate layer. Silently swallowing a failure can leave the application in a less trustworthy state than allowing the exception to propagate.

100884.sourceSearchName: c try catch statement c try catch statement
100884.title: C# Try-Catch Statement
100884.heading: Document

100885.sourceSearchName: c try catch statement c try catch statement
100885.title: C# Try-Catch Statement
100885.heading: C# Try-Catch Statement
100885.content:
A C# `try` block surrounds operations that may throw, and an associated `catch` block handles a compatible exception. When no exception occurs, execution leaves the `try` normally; when one occurs, control searches the available handlers rather than continuing through the remaining statements in the block.

The handler can inspect the exception, report useful context, choose a safe recovery, or rethrow it. A catch should represent a deliberate policy rather than a blanket promise that every failure is recoverable.

100886.sourceSearchName: c try catch statement c try catch statement
100886.title: C# Try-Catch Statement
100886.heading: References

100888.title: Unhandled Exception
100888.heading: Unhandled Exception
100888.content:
An unhandled exception is a runtime exception that reaches the top of an execution path without a matching handler. In a simple application, the runtime normally terminates the process and reports the exception and call stack.

The possibility of termination makes exception boundaries part of application design. Code should handle failures where it can preserve a valid state or add meaningful context, while allowing unrecoverable conditions to remain visible.

100890.sourceSearchName: multiple catch blocks multiple catch blocks
100890.title: Multiple Catch Blocks
100890.heading: Document

100891.sourceSearchName: multiple catch blocks multiple catch blocks
100891.title: Multiple Catch Blocks
100891.heading: Multiple Catch Blocks
100891.content:
Multiple catch blocks let one `try` statement apply different responses to different exception types. The runtime selects the first compatible handler, so specific exception handlers must appear before a general `Exception` handler.

This structure preserves information that would be lost in a single generic response. A missing file, invalid cast, and out-of-range index may require different messages, cleanup, or recovery even when they arise from the same operation.

100892.title: Multiple Catch Blocks
100892.heading: References

100894.sourceSearchName: c throw statement c throw statement
100894.title: C# Throw Statement
100894.heading: C# Throw Statement
100894.content:
The C# `throw` statement signals an exception deliberately. Code can create and throw an appropriate exception when a violated precondition or failed operation cannot be represented as an ordinary result.

Throwing transfers control to a compatible handler higher in the call chain. The chosen exception type and message should describe the failure precisely enough for that handler, a log, or a developer to understand the violated contract.

100897.sourceSearchName: c finally block c finally block
100897.title: C# Finally Block
100897.heading: C# Finally Block
100897.content:
A C# `finally` block runs when control leaves its associated `try`, whether the protected work succeeds or throws. It is intended for cleanup that must not depend on which catch block, if any, handles the failure.

Closing a manually managed database connection is a representative use: the resource should be released after both success and failure. Modern disposal constructs often express the same lifetime more directly, but the underlying guarantee remains deterministic cleanup.

100899.heading: Document

100900.sourceSearchName: built in .net exception types built in .net exception types
100900.title: Built-In .NET Exception Types
100900.heading: Built-In .NET Exception Types
100900.content:
Built-in .NET exception types classify familiar runtime failures so callers can distinguish them programmatically. Examples include `DivideByZeroException`, `IndexOutOfRangeException`, `InvalidCastException`, and `NullReferenceException`.

A specific type communicates more than a general `Exception` because it narrows the failed assumption and supports a targeted catch policy. The type does not replace a clear message or the surrounding operation's context.

100901.sourceSearchName: built in .net exception types built in .net exception types
100901.title: Built-In .NET Exception Types
100901.heading: References

100903.title: Custom Exception
100903.heading: Custom Exception
100903.content:
A custom exception is an application-defined type derived from `Exception` that names a failure not adequately represented by a built-in type. It can provide constructors for a message and an inner exception so callers retain both domain meaning and the original cause.

Creating a custom type is most useful when consumers need to catch that failure distinctly or when the name clarifies a stable application contract. It should not merely rename a standard exception without adding meaning.

100906.title: Exception Filter
100906.heading: Exception Filter
100906.content:
An exception filter adds a `when` condition to a C# catch clause. A handler is selected only when both the exception type and the filter expression match, allowing several handlers for the same type to express different policies.

Filters are useful when an exception carries a stable property that determines whether the current layer can handle it. Matching on fragile message text should be avoided when a typed property or error code is available.

100908.sourceSearchName: exception handling best practices exception handling best practices
100908.title: Exception Handling Best Practices
100908.heading: Document

100909.sourceSearchName: exception handling best practices exception handling best practices
100909.title: Exception Handling Best Practices
100909.heading: Exception Handling Best Practices
100909.content:
Exception handling should catch the most specific failure a layer can meaningfully address, use cleanup guarantees for dependent resources, and provide clear diagnostic messages. A custom exception is appropriate when the application needs a stable domain-specific failure contract.

Handling should happen close enough to preserve context but not so early that the code can only hide the problem. General catch blocks require an explicit fallback policy, and cleanup must run even when recovery is impossible.

100916.title: Object Collaboration
100916.heading: Object Collaboration
100916.content:
Object collaboration is the way objects use relationships and messages to complete behavior that no isolated object provides alone. Designing a system requires identifying which objects participate, what each one owns, and how their responsibilities connect.

The relationship type matters because a temporary use, a long-lived association, a whole-part structure, and inheritance create different coupling and lifetime expectations. [[UML Class Diagram|Class diagrams]] can make those choices visible before or alongside code.

100919.heading: Unified Modeling Language
100919.content:
The Unified Modeling Language is a standardized visual language for communicating software models. Its diagrams provide shared notation for structure and behavior so developers, architects, and stakeholders can discuss a system without relying only on prose or implementation code.

UML contains multiple diagram types rather than one universal view. A [[UML Class Diagram]] emphasizes static structure, a [[UML Use Case Diagram]] emphasizes functional scope, and a [[UML Sequence Diagram]] emphasizes interactions over time.

100922.title: UML Structural Diagram
100922.heading: UML Structural Diagram
100922.content:
A UML structural diagram describes the relatively stable organization of a system: its classes, objects, components, packages, deployment nodes, or other elements and their relationships. It answers what exists and how those parts are arranged.

The [[UML Class Diagram]] is the structural view most directly connected to object-oriented code. Behavioral diagrams complement it by showing how the represented parts participate in actions and interactions.

100924.heading: Document

100925.sourceSearchName: uml class diagram uml class diagram
100925.title: UML Class Diagram
100925.heading: UML Class Diagram
100925.content:
A UML class diagram is a structural model of classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships among them. It can guide implementation or document an existing object model by making important responsibilities and dependencies visible at a glance.

Each class is commonly drawn with separate name, attribute, and operation areas. Lines and endpoint symbols distinguish generalization, association, aggregation, composition, and dependency rather than treating every connection as equivalent.

100926.sourceSearchName: uml class diagram uml class diagram

100928.sourceSearchName: uml class diagram compartment uml class diagram compartment
100928.title: UML Class Diagram Compartment
100928.heading: UML Class Diagram Compartment
100928.content:
A class symbol in a UML class diagram is commonly divided into compartments for the class name, attributes, and operations. Attribute entries can show visibility, name, and type; operation entries can show visibility, parameters, and return type.

Separating these compartments lets the diagram convey both the identity of a class and the public or relevant structure it presents. A model can omit low-value detail when the diagram's purpose is architectural rather than implementation-level.

100931.sourceSearchName: uml generalization relationship uml generalization relationship
100931.title: UML Generalization Relationship
100931.heading: UML Generalization Relationship
100931.content:
A UML generalization relationship represents inheritance from a more specific classifier to a more general one. It is drawn as a solid line ending in a hollow triangle that points toward the superclass.

The notation communicates an is-a relationship: instances of the subclass are intended to satisfy the contract of the superclass while adding or specializing behavior. It should not be used merely because two classes share a few fields.

100932.sourceSearchName: uml generalization relationship uml generalization relationship
100932.title: UML Generalization Relationship
100932.heading: References

100933.sourceSearchName: uml association relationship uml association relationship
100933.title: UML Association Relationship
100933.heading: Document

100934.sourceSearchName: uml association relationship uml association relationship
100934.title: UML Association Relationship
100934.heading: UML Association Relationship
100934.content:
A UML association represents a meaningful structural connection between classifiers whose instances know about or relate to one another. A solid line connects the classes, and navigability arrows can indicate which direction can follow the relationship.

Association is the general relationship; [[UML Aggregation Relationship|aggregation]] and [[UML Composition Relationship|composition]] add whole-part semantics. The model should use the weakest relationship that accurately states the intended ownership and lifetime.

100935.sourceSearchName: uml association relationship uml association relationship
100935.title: UML Association Relationship

100937.sourceSearchName: uml aggregation relationship uml aggregation relationship
100937.title: UML Aggregation Relationship
100937.heading: UML Aggregation Relationship
100937.content:
Aggregation is a whole-part association in which the part can exist independently of the whole. UML marks the whole end of the association with a hollow diamond.

A computer and replaceable components illustrate the intended lifetime distinction: the whole refers to its parts, but destroying one object does not define the destruction of the other. Aggregation should be used only when that shared, independent ownership is important to the model.

100938.sourceSearchName: uml aggregation relationship uml aggregation relationship
100938.title: UML Aggregation Relationship
100938.heading: References

100939.sourceSearchName: uml composition relationship uml composition relationship
100939.title: UML Composition Relationship
100939.heading: Document

100940.sourceSearchName: uml composition relationship uml composition relationship
100940.title: UML Composition Relationship
100940.heading: UML Composition Relationship
100940.content:
Composition is a strong whole-part association in which the part's identity or useful lifetime belongs to the whole. UML marks the whole end with a filled diamond.

An order and its order items illustrate the relationship: the items are meaningful as constituents of that order rather than independently owned objects. Composition therefore communicates stronger ownership than [[UML Aggregation Relationship|aggregation]].

100941.title: UML Composition Relationship
100941.heading: References

100943.sourceSearchName: uml dependency relationship uml dependency relationship
100943.title: UML Dependency Relationship
100943.heading: UML Dependency Relationship
100943.content:
A UML dependency says one element uses or relies on another without necessarily retaining it as part of its structure. It is conventionally shown as a dashed directed line pointing toward the supplier.

A method parameter or temporary collaborator can create this relationship: changes to the supplier's contract may affect the dependent client, even though their instances do not share a whole-part lifetime. This distinguishes dependency from a stored [[UML Association Relationship|association]].

100977.heading: Visual Studio Call Stack
100977.content:
The Visual Studio Call Stack window lists the active chain of method calls that led to the current paused location. It helps identify which caller selected a path when the same method can be reached from several sources.

Moving among frames exposes each frame's source location and context. The stack explains control flow at one instant and is especially valuable when paired with an exception or [[Breakpoint]].

100980.content:
The Visual Studio Watch window repeatedly evaluates selected variables or expressions while execution is paused. It keeps important state visible across debugging steps without requiring the developer to hover over each value again.

Watching a small set of values can expose when an invariant first changes. Complex property evaluations may execute code, so they should be chosen carefully when side effects or evaluation cost matter.

100983.heading: Visual Studio Refactoring Tools
100983.content:
Visual Studio refactoring tools change code structure while preserving intended behavior across known references. Supported operations include renaming symbols, reordering or removing parameters, encapsulating a field as a property, and extracting selected statements into a method.

Semantic tooling is safer than isolated text replacement because it understands symbol use across the solution. Tests and review remain necessary because a mechanically consistent change can still alter reflection, serialization, or external contracts.

100986.title: ADO.NET
100986.heading: ADO.NET
100986.content:
ADO.NET is the .NET data-access framework for connecting to database systems, executing commands, reading results, and transferring data into disconnected in-memory structures. Provider-specific classes share common abstractions while adapting to systems such as SQL Server or ODBC data sources.

Its core workflow connects through a configured connection, executes a command, and consumes the result through a reader, scalar, affected-row count, or data adapter. Resource lifetime and transaction boundaries remain explicit responsibilities.

100988.sourceSearchName: ado.net data provider ado.net data provider
100988.title: ADO.NET Data Provider
100988.heading: Document

100989.sourceSearchName: ado.net data provider ado.net data provider
100989.title: ADO.NET Data Provider
100989.heading: ADO.NET Data Provider
100989.content:
An ADO.NET data provider is a coordinated set of classes for a particular database access mechanism. It supplies compatible connection, command, data reader, parameter, and data adapter implementations derived from common .NET abstractions.

Provider-specific types such as SQL Server and ODBC classes differ in details but preserve the same overall workflow. Selecting a provider therefore chooses both the database protocol and the concrete objects used to execute it.

100992.sourceSearchName: ado.net command object ado.net command object
100992.title: ADO.NET Command Object
100992.heading: ADO.NET Command Object
100992.content:
An ADO.NET command object represents an instruction to execute through a database connection. Its command text and command type can identify SQL text, a stored procedure, or another provider-supported form, while parameters carry external values.

Different execution methods express different expected results: [[ADO.NET ExecuteReader]] returns rows, [[ADO.NET ExecuteNonQuery]] reports affected rows, and [[ADO.NET ExecuteScalar]] returns one value.

100994.heading: Document

100995.sourceSearchName: ado.net execute reader ado.net execute reader
100995.title: ADO.NET ExecuteReader
100995.heading: ADO.NET ExecuteReader
100995.content:
`ExecuteReader` runs a database command expected to return rows and produces an [[ADO.NET DataReader]]. The caller advances through the forward-only result and retrieves each column by ordinal or name.

This path suits streamed result processing when the application does not need a disconnected, editable in-memory table. The reader and its connection must remain available until consumption finishes.

100996.sourceSearchName: ado.net execute reader ado.net execute reader
100996.title: ADO.NET ExecuteReader
100996.heading: References

100997.heading: Document

100998.sourceSearchName: ado.net execute non query ado.net execute non query
100998.title: ADO.NET ExecuteNonQuery
100998.heading: ADO.NET ExecuteNonQuery
100998.content:
`ExecuteNonQuery` runs a command that does not return a row result set, commonly an insert, update, delete, or stored procedure. Its integer result reports the number of rows affected when the provider can supply that information.

The count helps verify the command's effect, such as distinguishing one updated row from an unexpectedly broad update. It is an execution result, not by itself proof that a larger transaction was committed.

101000.heading: Document

101001.sourceSearchName: ado.net execute scalar ado.net execute scalar
101001.title: ADO.NET ExecuteScalar
101001.heading: ADO.NET ExecuteScalar
101001.content:
`ExecuteScalar` runs a database command and returns the first column of the first result row as one value. It avoids constructing a row-reading loop when the query asks for a count, aggregate, identifier, or another single result.

The caller must still handle database nulls and convert the returned object to the expected .NET type. A query intended for this method should make the single-value contract explicit.

101004.sourceSearchName: ado.net data reader ado.net data reader
101004.title: ADO.NET DataReader
101004.heading: ADO.NET DataReader
101004.content:
An ADO.NET data reader provides forward-only access to rows returned by a command. Calling `Read()` advances to the next row, and typed accessors or column indexes retrieve its values.

The reader is efficient for sequential processing because it does not first materialize the entire result into an editable table. It remains connected to the command's data source, so it should be consumed and closed within a clear resource lifetime.

101006.heading: Document

101007.sourceSearchName: ado.net data adapter ado.net data adapter
101007.title: ADO.NET DataAdapter
101007.heading: ADO.NET DataAdapter
101007.content:
An ADO.NET data adapter bridges a provider's connected commands and a disconnected `DataSet` or `DataTable`. `Fill` loads rows, `FillSchema` loads schema information, and `Update` can transfer supported in-memory changes back to the data source.

The disconnected object does not need to retain connection details while callers inspect or edit its data. The adapter still owns the mapping and command rules required to reconcile those changes with the database.

101009.heading: Document

101010.sourceSearchName: ado.net data set ado.net data set
101010.title: ADO.NET DataSet
101010.heading: ADO.NET DataSet
101010.content:
An ADO.NET `DataSet` is a disconnected in-memory container for one or more data tables and their relationships. A [[ADO.NET DataAdapter|data adapter]] can populate it from a provider, after which code can work with the data without holding the database connection open.

This model favors editable, transportable tabular state over the sequential streaming of an [[ADO.NET DataReader]]. Reconnecting changes to the data source requires explicit adapter commands and conflict-aware update behavior.

101015.title: Adapter Pattern
101015.heading: Adapter Pattern
101015.content:
The Adapter pattern places a translating object between a client and an incompatible interface. The client keeps using the contract it expects, while the adapter converts those calls and values into the form supplied by the existing component.

This preserves both sides from invasive changes and permits a different adapter for another implementation. The pattern is most useful when the mismatch is stable and translation is clearer than forcing either component to adopt the other's interface.

101018.title: Facade Pattern
101018.heading: Facade Pattern
101018.content:
The Facade pattern provides a simple entry point to a more complex group of collaborating objects. A client asks the facade for a higher-level operation, and the facade coordinates the lower-level calls required to fulfill it.

The pattern reduces the client's knowledge of subsystem structure without preventing advanced callers from using the subsystem directly when appropriate. The facade should express coherent tasks rather than merely becoming a new container for unrelated logic.

101021.title: Proxy Pattern
101021.heading: Proxy Pattern
101021.content:
The Proxy pattern places a stand-in object in front of another object and preserves a compatible access surface. The proxy controls when or how the real subject is reached, such as enforcing authorization, delaying an expensive operation, or isolating a third-party component.

Unlike an [[Adapter Pattern|adapter]], a proxy normally preserves the subject's conceptual interface rather than translating to a different one. Its added control should remain visible enough that callers understand latency, security, or lifetime effects.

101023.title: Version Control System

101024.sourceSearchName: version control system version control system
101024.title: Version Control System
101024.heading: Version Control System
101024.content:
A version control system records changes to a collection of files so collaborators can identify revisions, compare work, and recover earlier states. Each recorded revision gives a project a shared history instead of relying on manually copied backup folders.

Version control also coordinates concurrent development by making each contribution and merge explicit. Git is distributed, so a local repository contains history and supports most revision operations without a network connection.

101027.sourceSearchName: git working tree state git working tree state
101027.title: Git Working Tree State
101027.heading: Git Working Tree State
101027.content:
Git distinguishes changes in the working tree from content staged for the next commit and content already committed to repository history. A file may therefore be modified without being selected for the next snapshot.

This separation lets a developer prepare a coherent commit from only part of the current work. [[Git Status]] exposes the state of tracked, untracked, modified, and staged paths before history is changed.

101029.sourceSearchName: git staging area git staging area
101029.title: Git Staging Area
101029.heading: Document

101030.sourceSearchName: git staging area git staging area
101030.title: Git Staging Area
101030.heading: Git Staging Area
101030.content:
The Git staging area is the proposed content of the next commit. [[Git Add]] copies selected working-tree changes into this index, allowing other local edits to remain outside the snapshot.

Staging is a review boundary between editing and committing. A developer can inspect and adjust the selected changes so the resulting [[Git Commit]] represents one understandable unit of work.

101031.sourceSearchName: git staging area git staging area
101031.title: Git Staging Area
101031.heading: References

101033.title: Git Commit
101033.heading: Git Commit
101033.content:
A Git commit records the staged snapshot together with metadata such as its message, author information, and parent commit. Its hash identifies the resulting history object.

Only staged content enters the commit; unrelated working-tree changes remain outside it. A clear message explains the purpose of the snapshot so [[Git Log|history inspection]] reveals decisions rather than only file differences.

101036.title: Git Configuration
101036.heading: Git Configuration
101036.content:
Git configuration stores settings that affect repository behavior and commit identity, including the user's name and email. Settings can be global for the user or overridden within one repository.

`git config --list` displays effective entries, while scoped commands add or change them. Repository-specific configuration is useful when one project needs an identity or behavior different from the user's general defaults.

101038.sourceSearchName: git repository initialization git repository initialization
101038.title: Git Repository Initialization
101038.heading: Document

101039.sourceSearchName: git repository initialization git repository initialization
101039.title: Git Repository Initialization
101039.heading: Git Repository Initialization
101039.content:
`git init` creates Git repository metadata for an existing directory. The new `.git` directory holds the object database, references, configuration, and other information required to record history locally.

Initialization does not automatically create a commit from every file. The developer still reviews the working tree, stages intended paths, and creates the first snapshot.

101040.sourceSearchName: git repository initialization git repository initialization
101040.title: Git Repository Initialization
101040.heading: References

101042.title: Git Clone
101042.heading: Git Clone
101042.content:
`git clone` creates a local repository from an existing repository location. The result includes a working tree, commit history, branches and tags available from the source, and remote configuration for later synchronization.

Cloning differs from downloading only the current files because it preserves the repository's version-control data. Local commits can then be created offline and later exchanged with the configured remote.

101045.title: Git Status
101045.heading: Git Status
101045.content:
`git status` summarizes the current branch and the relationship among the working tree, staging area, and current commit. It identifies untracked paths, unstaged modifications, and changes selected for the next commit.

The command is a safety check before staging, committing, or switching work. It does not change repository state and should be used to verify what Git currently sees.

101048.title: Git Add
101048.heading: Git Add
101048.content:
`git add` places selected working-tree content into the [[Git Staging Area]]. It can stage a named file, a directory, or a broader set of paths for inclusion in the next commit.

The command stages the content as it exists at that moment; later edits to the same file are not automatically included. Reviewing the staged diff prevents accidental selection of unrelated or sensitive changes.

101051.title: Git Log
101051.heading: Git Log
101051.content:
`git log` displays commits reachable through repository history. A log entry can show the commit hash, author, date, message, and relationships to branches or parent commits.

History inspection helps identify when and why a change entered the codebase. Formatting and filtering options can narrow the view by path, author, time, or graph structure without modifying the repository.

101054.title: Git Remote
101054.heading: Git Remote
101054.content:
A Git remote is a local name for another repository location used to exchange refs and objects. `origin` is a common default name created by cloning, but a repository can define multiple remotes.

`git remote -v` displays configured fetch and push URLs, while `git remote add` creates a new mapping. The remote name is only an alias; synchronization still occurs through explicit fetch, pull, or push operations.

101057.title: Git Push
101057.heading: Git Push
101057.content:
`git push` sends local objects and updates selected references in a remote repository. A typical invocation identifies a remote and a local branch whose commits should become reachable from a remote branch.

Push transfers committed history, not merely every current working-tree edit. The remote may reject an update when policy, permissions, file limits, or conflicting history prevents the requested reference change.

101060.title: Git Pull
101060.heading: Git Pull
101060.content:
`git pull` obtains updates from a remote and integrates them into the current local branch according to the configured strategy. It combines the retrieval step of [[Git Fetch]] with a merge or rebase operation.

Because it can change the checked-out branch, pull is not merely a status check. Inspecting local changes and understanding the chosen integration policy helps avoid an unexpected merge or conflict.

101063.title: Git Fetch
101063.heading: Git Fetch
101063.content:
`git fetch` downloads objects and updates remote-tracking references without integrating them into the current branch. It lets a developer inspect the remote history before deciding how to combine it with local work.

This separation distinguishes fetch from [[Git Pull]]. After fetching, an explicit merge, rebase, or other comparison can be performed with the now-current remote-tracking branch.

101066.title: Git Branch
101066.heading: Git Branch
101066.content:
A Git branch is a movable reference to a commit. Creating a branch records a lightweight name for a line of development rather than copying the entire working directory and history.

New commits advance the currently checked-out branch, while other branch references remain at their previous commits. Branches let related work develop independently until [[Git Merge|integration]] or another history operation combines it.

101069.title: Git HEAD
101069.heading: Git HEAD
101069.content:
Git `HEAD` identifies the currently checked-out branch or, in a detached state, a specific commit. It tells Git which history position the working tree represents and where a new commit will normally attach.

When a branch is checked out and a commit is created, that branch reference advances and `HEAD` continues to point through it. Commands that switch commits therefore change both the visible files and the context for later history operations.

101072.title: Git Checkout
101072.heading: Git Checkout
101072.content:
`git checkout` can switch the working tree and `HEAD` to another branch or commit. In the workflow described by the source, `git checkout -b name` creates a branch and immediately switches to it.

Switching can overwrite the working-tree representation, so conflicting uncommitted changes must be resolved or preserved first. Newer Git versions also provide more focused switch and restore commands, but checkout remains a historical combined interface.

101075.title: Git Merge
101075.heading: Git Merge
101075.content:
`git merge` integrates the history of another branch into the currently checked-out branch. Git either advances the current reference when no divergence exists or creates a merge result that joins the parent histories.

When both lines changed incompatible portions of the same content, the developer must resolve conflicts before completing the merge. The operation should be run from the branch intended to receive the other branch's work.
